newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Uphill revenue battle seen in S.African budget.
newsitem.headline: Uphill revenue battle seen in S.African budget.

text.p: Finance Minister Trevor Manuel faces an uphill revenue collection battle in 1997/98, even assuming real spending cuts, the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said.

Director of economic policy Ben van Rensburg told reporters he expected expenditure of 189 billion rand in the 1997/98 budget due to be presented on Wednesday, representing a real cut of 1.2 percent from the current year's spending total of 176 billion.

To achieve the goal of a four percent deficit, or 25 billion rand, would require revenue of 164 billion rand, up from 147 billion. But Manuel would need to spend an extra 6.5 billion to correct for "bracket creep" and other inequities on income tax.

"Tax increases and more efficiency of collection will therefore be needed...this will require creative thinking in squeezing that much more out of the system without jeopardising the (economic) upswing," van Rensburg said.

With a hike in value added tax (VAT) from the current 14 percent level a "no go" for political reasons, the fear must be that Manuel might look to some kind of capital gains tax, land tax or additional retirement fund tax to bridge the budget gap, he said.
Such taxes on investment would send the wrong message at a time when the govenment needed to do more to promote savings in the South African economy, he argued.
Overall, Sacob expected a positive budget which would underscore that the government remained committed to achieving deficit reduction, the central plank of its macro-economic strategy.
But the manner in which the target was achieved would also be crucial for the markets, van Rensburg said.
Van Rensburg said Manuel would have to address the issue of foreign exchange controls in the budget, given recent intense speculation on the issue.

The minister was mostly likely to lay out a timetable for the phased removal of controls on blocked rand funds of emigrants -- totalling some 15 billion rand -- possibly via the issue of special bonds which would let them take money out after a period of years.
